planting.note: Root 4-6 inch softwood tip cuttings in spring or early summer and set rooted plants out after frost danger has passed into humus-rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Ribbon bush is a fast-growing South African shrub grown for its late-summer and autumn spikes of narrow, violet-purple tubular flowers that draw bees and sunbirds; it performs best in morning sun with afternoon shade or dappled woodland light, in soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged. Propagate by rooting softwood cuttings rather than seed, since named forms come true only from cuttings, and pinch young plants to encourage branching before the first flower spikes form. Where winter temperatures dip into the low 20s F the top growth dies back, so cut stems to the ground in late winter and mulch the crown; farther south it persists as a woody perennial that benefits from a hard spring pruning to prevent legginess. Its dense habit and long autumn bloom window make it a useful filler toward the back of a part-shade border or woodland edge.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Splash Select Pink Polka Dot Plant

planting.note: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, pressing it into the surface of moist mix without covering, then transplant into partial to full shade once nights stay warm.

directions: Splash Select Pink is a seed-grown polka dot plant strain bred for a more upright, vigorous habit than the compact Confetti types, with broad green leaves heavily overlaid in rose-pink speckling that reads almost solid pink from a distance in good light. Start seed indoors under lights since germination is slow in cool soil, then move transplants into humus-rich, evenly moist beds or containers in partial to full shade after frost danger passes. Pinch stems through the season to keep plants bushy and pop off the small lavender flower spikes that appear as days shorten, since blooming diverts energy from leaf color and signals the plant is winding down. Treated as a tender perennial in zones 10-12 and as a warm-season annual elsewhere, it combines well with ferns and caladiums in a shaded container or bed.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Splash Select White Polka Dot Plant

planting.note: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, pressing it into the surface of moist mix without covering, then transplant into partial to full shade once nights stay warm.

directions: Splash Select White carries dense, creamy-white speckling over a dark green ground that brightens deep-shade plantings more than any other color form of this seed series, making it a favorite for lighting up woodland containers or shaded entryway beds. Start seed indoors under lights, since cool soil slows germination noticeably, then harden off and transplant into humus-rich, evenly moist soil after the last frost. Pinch growing tips regularly through the season to keep the taller Splash Select habit from flopping, and remove flower spikes as they form to keep the plant channeling energy into foliage rather than seed set. It is grown as a tender perennial in zones 10-12 and everywhere else as a reliable warm-season annual that pairs well with dark-leaved companions like coleus or Persian shield for strong contrast.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Splash Select Red Polka Dot Plant

planting.note: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, pressing it into the surface of moist mix without covering, then transplant into partial to full shade once nights stay warm.

directions: Splash Select Red is the most dramatic color in this seed-grown polka dot plant series, with leaves washed in deep crimson-red blotches over a green base; the red pigment holds its intensity best with a bit more light than the pink or white forms tolerate, so give it bright indirect light or a few hours of gentle morning sun rather than deep shade. Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out once nights stay warm, into humus-rich soil that is kept evenly moist but never soggy. Pinch regularly to maintain a bushy, upright form and remove the small lavender flower spikes that appear late in the season, since letting the plant flower and set seed shortens its productive foliage display. It is grown as a tender perennial in zones 10-12 and as a warm-season bedding or container annual elsewhere, offering the strongest color echo for red- and burgundy-themed shade plantings.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
